method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. claims.claim: **The most common cause in adolescents is anovulatory cycles.** ⚠️ **Pregnancy-related bleeding and bleeding disorders are important differentials.**
claims.source_text: The most common cause of heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) in adolescents is anovulatory cycles … Pregnancy-related bleeding and bleeding disorders are important differentials to consider
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Excessive flow** = more than 7 days or more than 80 mL per cycle · changing a super pad/tampon more often than every 2 hours · symptomatic anaemia · lifestyle disturbance.
claims.source_text: Excessive menstrual flow is defined as any of the following >7 days duration or >80 mL per cycle bleeding necessitating changing a super pad/tampon more than every 2 hours causing symptomatic anaemia causing lifestyle disturbance
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Causes to consider:** pregnancy (miscarriage, ectopic, gestational trophoblastic disease); **von Willebrand disease**, platelet function disorder, thrombocytopenia; thyroid dysfunction, PCOS; hormonal contraception and anticoagulants.
claims.source_text: Pregnancy: miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, gestational trophoblastic disease … Haematological: von Willebrand Disease, platelet function disorder, thrombocytopenia, other bleeding disorder … Endocrine: anovulatory cycles (most common cause in adolescence), thyroid dysfunction, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) … Medication: hormonal contraception, anticoagulants
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severity:** mild — slightly or moderately increased flow, normal haemoglobin · moderate — menses every 1–3 weeks, moderate–heavy flow, haemoglobin reduced but at least 100 g/L · ⚠️ **severe — haemoglobin under 100 g/L and/or haemodynamic instability.**
claims.source_text: Mild Slightly or moderately increased menstrual flow with normal haemoglobin Moderate Moderately prolonged or frequent menses (every 1–3 weeks), with moderate to heavy flow and reduced haemoglobin (≥100 g/L) Severe Heavy bleeding with haemoglobin <100 g/L and/or haemodynamic instability
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Vaginal examination is rarely indicated in an adolescent**; discuss with a senior clinician, and if needed perform it only once.
claims.source_text: Vaginal examination is rarely indicated in an adolescent. It should be discussed with a senior clinician, and if needed should only be performed once
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider FBE, ferritin, coagulation screen, TSH and βhCG (with consent)**; group and hold if bleeding is severe.
claims.source_text: Consider FBE Ferritin Coagulation screen TSH Urine or blood ßhCG (with consent) Blood group and antibody screen if severe bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected bleeding disorder: consider PFA-100 and a von Willebrand screen — not during acute bleeding or after recent NSAID use.**
claims.source_text: If a bleeding disorder is suspected, consider platelet function assay (PFA) 100 and von Willebrand screen. These tests should not be done during acute bleeding or with recent NSAID use
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pelvic ultrasound is rarely required** — only for atypical features or a palpable mass.
claims.source_text: Pelvic ultrasound is rarely required. Consider if there are atypical features or a palpable mass
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild:** if contraception is not wanted, reassure and observe; consider regular NSAIDs and tranexamic acid during menses. **Moderate:** tranexamic acid during menses plus oral progestogen-only or combined oral contraceptive pill.
claims.source_text: Mild If no desire for contraception, provide reassurance and observation Consider non-hormonal management such as regular NSAIDs and tranexamic acid during menses Moderate Tranexamic acid during menses Hormonal therapy: Oral progesterone-only hormone therapy or Combination oestrogen-progesterone oral contraceptive pills
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe:** consider pregnancy or a bleeding disorder; IV access, resuscitation, tranexamic acid, hormonal therapy (e.g. high-dose norethisterone); iron infusion, or packed red cells if haemodynamically unstable despite fluids; **gynaecology review and consider inpatient observation.**
claims.source_text: Severe Consider other causes such as pregnancy or bleeding disorder IV access Resuscitation Tranexamic acid Hormonal therapy eg high dose norethisterone Iron infusion as required or packed red blood cells (PRBC) if haemodynamic instability despite fluid resuscitation. See blood product prescription Specialist review (gynaecology) and consider inpatient observation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider iron supplementation** and a menstrual calendar or app.
claims.source_text: Consider iron supplementation … Consider a menstrual calendar or app
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tranexamic acid 15–25 mg/kg (max 1 g) 2–3 times a day on heavy days** — cuts flow by 25–50%.
claims.source_text: Tranexamic acid 15-25 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) 2-3 times a day for days of heavy bleeding can decrease flow by 25-50%
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **NSAIDs taken regularly during menstruation** (e.g. mefenamic acid 500 mg tds, naproxen 500 mg bd) reduce flow and can be combined with tranexamic acid.
claims.source_text: NSAIDs (eg mefenamic acid 500 mg tds, naproxen 500 mg bd) can decrease flow if taken regularly during menstruation. NSAIDs can be used in conjunction with tranexamic acid
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Active bleeding:** norethisterone 5–10 mg three times daily for 10 days, then wean slowly (e.g. by 5 mg/week) **or** medroxyprogesterone acetate 10–20 mg tds for 10 days, then stop or continue 10 mg daily.
claims.source_text: Use in active bleeding Norethisterone 5-10 mg can be taken 3 times daily for 10 days then weaned slowly (eg by 5 mg/week) … Alternatively, medroxyprogesterone acetate 10-20 mg tds for 10 days then cease or continue with 10 mg daily prophylactic treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Stopping progestogen-only treatment abruptly will precipitate bleeding.** Seek specialist advice for higher doses or non-response.
claims.source_text: if progesterone-only treatment is stopped abruptly this will precipitate bleeding … seek specialist advice for higher doses or patients not responding to initial treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylaxis:** norethisterone 5–10 mg or medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily continuously · depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks · Mirena LNG-IUD 5–8-yearly.
claims.source_text: Prophylactic treatment Norethisterone 5-10 mg or medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily taken continuously Depot medroxyprogesterone-acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks Mirena (levonorgestrel intrauterine device) 5-8 yearly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The COC can cut flow by 50%**; usually start low-dose oestrogen with moderate progestin (e.g. ethinylestradiol 30 microg + levonorgestrel 150 microg). Check contraindications.
claims.source_text: Combined oestrogen and progestin oral contraceptive pill can decrease flow by 50% and is effective for anovulation or irregular menses. Often started with a low dose oestrogen and moderate progestin (eg ethinylestradiol 30 microg + levonorgestrel 150 microg). See Contraindications
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Active bleeding:** one pill every eight hours until bleeding stops (usually within 48 hours), then one pill every 12 hours for 3 days, then one daily continuously until outpatient review.
claims.source_text: Use in active bleeding One pill every eight hours until bleeding stops (usually within 48 hours), then One pill every 12 hours for 3 days, then One pill daily continuously until outpatient review with GP or gynaecology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylaxis:** one pill daily; move to continuous use after the first month's withdrawal bleed.
claims.source_text: Prophylactic treatment One oral contraceptive pill daily Transition to continuous use after the first month's withdrawal bleed
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **GP or paediatrician review in 2 weeks** to confirm active bleeding has resolved; after starting maintenance, **review in 3–4 months.**
claims.source_text: GP or paediatrician in 2 weeks to ensure resolution of active bleeding … After commencement of maintenance therapy, follow up in 3-4 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Involve gynaecology for:** severe bleeding · haemodynamic instability · symptomatic anaemia · haemoglobin under 100 g/L · no response to tranexamic acid and/or hormonal treatment.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with gynaecology team when Features of severe bleeding Haemodynamically unstable Symptomatic anaemia Haemoglobin <100 g/L Not responding to empiric treatment with tranexamic acid and/or hormonal treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when stable with review booked:** within a month for mild bleeding, **within 48 hours for ongoing heavy bleeding.**
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when Stable, and a review is scheduled within a month for mild bleeding within 48 hours for ongoing heavy bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23
